claims.statement: Evaluation has three distinct run-selection paths: a callable target creates prediction runs, Python can rescore one existing experiment without predicting, and comparative evaluation scores corresponding runs from existing experiments.

New-target evaluation resolves dataset names, dataset IDs, and supplied example iterables, expands examples by `num_repetitions`, and, when uploading, creates an experiment tied to the reference dataset and finalizes it with dataset version and split metadata.
Each new-target prediction is traced under the experiment and associated with its reference example and example version, which supplies the join between runs and dataset examples.

Python supports `upload_results=False` only for new-target evaluation: it omits remote experiment creation, finalization, and feedback uploads while retaining local rows and scores; existing and comparative targets reject this mode.

Concurrency zero means sequential execution; Python pipelines work with context-aware thread or async scheduling, while JavaScript can use separate target and evaluator queues when both specific limits are supplied or one shared queue otherwise.

Prediction and row evaluation are pipelined so completed predictions can be scored before slower predictions finish; JavaScript demonstrates this with separate target/evaluator queues and restores expanded dataset order before final rows and summary evaluation, while Python result iterators expose completion order.

Plain evaluator functions are adapted to the `RunEvaluator` interface, their one-or-many result forms are normalized, and evaluator traces supply source run IDs that connect feedback to its generating computation.
Row evaluators create feedback against target runs, while summary evaluators run after collecting all aligned runs/examples and create project-level feedback with no target run ID.

Ordinary row and summary evaluator failures are isolated per evaluator: both SDKs log and continue, Python additionally emits keyed error feedback when feedback keys can be inferred, and JavaScript leaves the failed evaluator result absent.

Python existing-experiment evaluation loads the experiment's runs and reloads examples from its reference dataset at the stored dataset version; in both SDKs nested loading reconstructs child-run trees while returning roots for scoring.

Comparative evaluation requires multiple experiments on the same reference dataset and at least one comparator, intersects runs by reference example, optionally randomizes run order, creates a comparative experiment, and uploads per-run scores linked to it.

Python rejects path-incompatible options for existing and comparative targets, requires data for new callable targets, rejects simultaneous `experiment` and `experiment_prefix`, and does not support comparative evaluation through `aevaluate`.

Target exceptions are logged per item; Python's `error_handling='log'` associates failed traces with the example while `'ignore'` associates only successful traces, and JavaScript raises if the trace wrapper failed to create any run and attempts project finalization even after prediction failure.

Python provides caller-visible streaming when `blocking=False` through a background thread or async processing task, whereas JavaScript's `evaluate` currently consumes and orders every row, computes summaries, and flushes pending trace batches before resolving its iterable result.
Comparative evaluator errors fail the aggregate comparative call rather than being isolated like ordinary row evaluator errors.

Setting `disable_evaluator_tracing` or `disableEvaluatorTracing` for ordinary evaluation suppresses evaluator traces and removes evaluator source-run links without suppressing row or summary scores and feedback; target tracing is unaffected.

Evaluator tracing defaults are not fully symmetric: JavaScript summary evaluation leaves the tracing override unset when suppression is omitted so environment configuration remains authoritative, while JavaScript row evaluation and uploaded Python evaluation explicitly enable evaluator tracing unless suppression is requested; Python local evaluation uses local tracing.

Comparative implementations deliberately differ: JavaScript supports two or more source experiments, rejects an empty common-example intersection, warns on dataset-version differences, and validates returned run IDs; Python top-level dispatch accepts exactly two experiments and its helper does not perform those equivalent checks.
